questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer:
It was easy to find a house, but I was also quick.
I started messaging a lot of people on Airbnb already the day after I was accepted, because I had heard it could be difficult to find a place to live. I got in touch with a man who owns several houses around Victoria and rented a long-term place from him.
I knew three girls from home who had also been accepted to UVic, and I asked if they wanted to live with me, so we rented it together.
Everyone I’ve met on exchange who lived off-campus has lived with roommates. There were a couple of people who weren’t fast enough, so they stayed in our living room for the first few weeks until they found a place.
I would recommend looking at Neighbor:
https://neighbour.townline.com/

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: Start finding a place as soon as possible and be prepared to live with roommates

questions.answer: ICS exchange team, tutors and informationcenter - all really helpfuld and friendly

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer:
I got all the courses I wanted without any problems.

During the first week I wanted to change some of my courses, and it was super quick and easy. I emailed the professors of the courses I wanted to switch to, and they handled the rest for me. Even for courses I didn’t have the prerequisites for, I just wrote that I was interested in joining, and I was given a spot

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Send emails! All the professors are super kind and helpful.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: Both

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer:
The courses are definitely easier than what I’m used to at the UCPH. I didn’t go for the academic challenge, and I chose my classes based on wanting a lot of free time to travel. So I chose online courses or courses that were recorded, so I could watch the lectures whenever I wanted.

However, I do know that a few of my friends chose courses that were much more demanding than what they were used to.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer:
The teaching style is quite different from UCPH. I’m used to attending lectures, keeping up, and then only stressing during the exam period, where I basically shut myself in and study nonstop.

At UVic, the structure is very different, with lots of assignments and midterms throughout the semester that count toward a large part of the final grade.

At first, I found it a bit annoying, but I actually ended up liking it because it took a lot of pressure off the final exam, which was really nice. I had completed so much of the required work during the semester that technically, I didn’t even need to pass my final exams to pass the courses

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your second semester. *
What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
I was really burnt out from studying when I left, so I ended up switching to courses that weren’t very related to my degree - which was amazing!

Ceramics turned out to be my most demanding course because I had to spend a lot of time in the studio working on assignments, but it was an incredible creative break and I highly recommend it.

I also took an English course, and I’ve never experienced anything like it. My professor was absolutely phenomenal, and I wish everyone could take a class with him!

In general, UVic offers a lot of courses outside the usual academic fields, and I definitely recommend taking advantage of that

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
I bought a car in the first week, and that’s definitely my biggest recommendation! While it’s possible to get around by bike or bus, I found it to be a bit tricky and honestly, biking can be pretty scary in Victoria at times.

Having a car made life so much easier. We used it for everything: grocery shopping (which is a bit far by bike or bus), exploring the island, and even heading to the mainland. Used cars are really cheap on Marketplace, so in the end, three of us bought one each for our whole group of friends, making it much easier to go on trips together.

It turned out to be a big win for the clubs at UVic as well, since we could contribute by providing transportation for surf trips and other group activities.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
An absolute must is the trip to the mainland, driving from Banff to Jasper! It’s hands down one of the most beautiful journeys I’ve ever taken.

Make sure to take a weekend trip to Salt Spring Island - don’t miss the Saturday market.

Tofino is a top spot for surfing! It’s pricey, but definitely worth it. While you're there, also check out Ucluelet, which is nearby and equally amazing.

Strathcona National Park is stunning! If you’re into hiking, tackle either King’s Peak or the Landslide Trail. On the way back, be sure to stop at Campbell River to swim with the salmon during salmon season - it’s a pretty unique experience.

Telegraph Cove, located on the northern part of Vancouver Island, is a tiny, picturesque town. The waters around there are preserved for whales and orcas, so there’s an abundance of marine life.

I spent a month driving around the island before the semester started, and while it was beautiful, I wouldn’t recommend going farther north than Port McNeill - there’s not much to do beyond that point.

Victoria itself has a bunch of cozy bars and cool hangouts. We loved the board game café, and when we went out, we went to Darcies or  Lucky’s (they’ve got the best music on Mondays, which is when everyone goes out).

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: As soon as you get used to everyone wanting to small talk, it's really easy.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Canadians are very inviting, so don't hesitate to say yes - they do actually mean it

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Around Pandora Avenue, there are quite a few homeless people, which can be a bit shocking at first. However, I never had any uncomfortable experiences with anyone - it was more the initial surprise of seeing so many in one area.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The Canadian openness <3 Everyone is kind and friendly

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Get a place to live as soon as possible!

Take every opportunity to get out of the city and into nature - it’s absolutely incomparable.

When I started my exchange, my goal was to meet people from outside of Denmark. We had a group of 16 Danes at UVic, and honestly, the best thing that happened to me was meeting them. I met so many amazing Canadians and exchange students from around the world, but I’m incredibly grateful for the friendships I made with fellow Danes.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Don't be afraid to ask

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Exchange can be tough - so much fun, but also really challenging at times. That’s why having friends who speak the same language and understand exactly what you’re going through is so valuable. The fact that we can reunite back in Denmark and relive all those memories together is, without a doubt, the highlight of this journey for me.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer:
Something personal happened in my family back home. It was really difficult not being there, and not being able to help or talk about it with an ocean and a nine-hour time difference between us.

I’m very grateful that I had a strong support network during the exchange who helped me through it.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
